# 22 — The Crew: The Quest for Planet Nine

**Status:** **built and playing** (`game/games/the_crew.json`, generated by
`tools/make_the_crew.py`, tested by `tests/integration/the_crew.lua`) — three
seats, the full trick, the task deck and both instant-loss triggers. Left: the
communication token and the order tokens, and the reason the first one is not
cheap is worth reading · **Size:** medium · **Depends on:** none of the
deckbuilder candidates — self-contained

**The verdict below held — everything downstream of `set_active_seat` was
content — and building it turned up a clamp the engine was said not to have.**
See *What building it found* at the bottom.

> *Cooperative trick-taking. Named directly alongside the deckbuilder
> research as a good fit.*

**Objective.** The Crew is trick-taking stripped to its cleanest modern
form: four numbered suits plus a trump ("rocket") suit, no bidding, task
cards dealt out at the start of each of fifty missions ("I will win a trick
containing this card," "I will win exactly N tricks," some tasks partially
ordered relative to each other), and a once-per-mission communication token
that lets a player flag exactly one card in hand as highest/lowest/only-of-
suit. [01-boardgames.md](01-boardgames.md) already flagged the general shape
of this question — this file is where it gets checked against one real game:
**the trick winner becomes the next active seat**, which today's phase
routing (`"seat": "next"`) cannot express, since it only walks the fixed
seat list in file order.

---

## What shipped — the primitive, both halves

**`@owner_of.<scope>` is a scope, and it answers with the seats.** The lookup
this file identified as its one root — *convert "this entity's owner" into a seat
the rules can talk about* — exists now in `predicate.entities_in_scope`, spelled
as a prefix on a scope expression because the words after `@` are separated by
`.` and a colon would arrive as a second action argument. `score@owner_of.target`
is the score of whoever owns the card the player chose; on its own, `@owner_of`
is the acting card's own seat, which no card could name before.

Four things the build settled:

- **It answers with the seat's *card*, not a key**, because a scope's answer is
  entities everywhere else — and the card's `def_key` is the seat key, so the
  other half of the primitive reads it back off the same answer.
- **It uses `predicate.seat_of`, not `tags.owner_of`.** `seat_of` is what
  `mine`/`enemy` ask, so the scope and the owner words can never disagree about
  whose a card is; it also makes a seat card asked about itself answer itself
  rather than nobody.
- **An owner word means whichever side of the prefix it stands on** — inside it
  picks the cards (`@owner_of.enemy.creature`), before it it filters the seats
  that come back (`@mine.owner_of.target`). Each word sits beside what it is
  about, so neither reading has to be remembered.
- **Each seat answers once** however many cards it owns, and a card nobody owns
  names nobody. A seat counted once per card would pay a player twice for
  holding two pieces, which reads as a rules decision rather than as a bug.

**And the writing half is `set_active_seat:<scope>`**, an ordinary action, so
cards, zones and phases all reach it. Three things it decided:

- **The scope names cards and the seat is whose they are**, through the same
  `seat_of`. So `set_active_seat:target` and `set_active_seat:owner_of.target`
  say the same thing about an ordinary card, and naming a seat card picks that
  seat. One rule rather than two spellings for one intent.
- **Two seats is refused, none is not.** Picking the first of two would make
  turn order depend on the order cards sit in the file; a scope matching nothing
  is an ordinary state, because the trick is not won until somebody wins it.
- **A handover ends the undo history**, exactly as the end of a turn does —
  `actions.on_seat_change`, closed by `flow` at the bottom of the file, since
  `actions` may not require it.

It needed nothing from the network: the turn lives on the injected system card,
which is in the snapshot with everything else, so the far end learns whose turn
it is the way it learns the rest. `tests/integration/active_seat.lua` asserts
that over a real delta rather than assuming it.

The routing spelling — `"seat": "owner_of:<scope>"` on a phase's `next` entry —
was **not** built: the action covers the trick winner from inside the phase that
scores the trick, and nothing else asked. [Assumption: it stays unbuilt until a
game wants the seat decided by the routing rather than by an action, which no
researched game does.]

## The research, and what it predicted

[the_crew/rules.md](the_crew/rules.md) — built from the official KOSMOS rulebook
and mission logbook, both read in full, with every number not cross-confirmed
flagged in §11. One correction to this file's own framing came out of it: "win
exactly N tricks", "win no tricks" and the rest are **not** in the 36-card task
deck, which expresses exactly one shape ("win the trick containing this card",
optionally sequenced by an order token). The rest is per-mission rule text
printed in the logbook. Both systems are real and the doc covers both.

The gap pass then checked eighteen rules against the engine and found **one**
that had no answer: *the trick winner becomes the next active seat*. Everything
else was either already there or ordinary content, including the two the file
expected to be hard — follow-suit (the escape hatch does it, given a `needs`
comparing two subjects) and identifying the winner (a card comparing itself to
`max:` over the trick). That verdict held to the letter when it was built.

The prediction is not reproduced here. It was written against the struct
condition spelling that [17](17-conditions-as-expressions.md) has since deleted,
so as a worked example it now teaches a syntax that no longer parses — and what
it concluded is the sentence above.

---

## What building it found

`the_crew.json` is 1,512 lines from a 365-line generator: four seats, the
40-card deck, the 36-card task deck, the commander, the draft, ten tricks and
both instant-loss triggers. **The verdict above held exactly** —
`set_active_seat` was the only thing missing, and everything downstream of it
turned out to be content. What follows is the part a document could not have
predicted.

### The clamp at one exists after all, and Tough could have had it

[23](23-splendor.md) established that `stat_damage` against a floor of zero is
`max(0, a - b)`, and closed by saying that a clamp anywhere *but* at zero — LoR's
Tough, `min(1, damage)` — was still missing. **It is not.** A floor at zero gives
you both halves:

```
min(a, k) = a - max(0, a - k)
```

which is three actions and one scratch number with `min: 0`:

```json
"stat_set:over@self:sum:live@self",
"stat_damage:over@self:1",
"stat_damage:live@self:sum:over@self"
```

`k` may be any literal. **The floor is the only operator the grammar has, and it
is enough for both directions.**

The Crew needed it because a rocket led is *both* the suit that was followed and
the trump, so the two flags added to two and had to come back to one — and that
is no longer why. Adding the flags was an **or** written as arithmetic, and
[26](26-an-if-and-a-name.md) gave an ability a `when`, so it is two abilities
now and this game uses neither clamp. The identity is still true and still the
only one there is; `tests/integration/the_crew.lua` asserts it over two ordinary
floored stats rather than through a rule that depends on it.

**And Tough does not even need that much.** [18](18-legends-of-runeterra.md)
reads the rule as `min(1, damage)` and concludes it cannot be written, so LoR
ships an approximation — strike for full power, then hand a point back if the
target is tough — which *heals* against a zero-power source. But the rule is
"reduce incoming damage by 1, never below 0", and that is `max(0, a - b)`, which
has been available since stats had floors. The reason it looked impossible is
that the subtraction was being attempted on the way *out*, after the damage had
landed. Done on a scratch number on the way in, it is three ordinary lines:

```json
"stat_set:hurt@self:sum:power@self",
"stat_damage:hurt@self:count:tough@across",
"stat_damage:health@across:sum:hurt@self"
```

with `hurt` declared `min: 0`. **No replacement effect, no trigger subsystem** —
18 was right that a replacement effect is the general answer and wrong that this
case needs one. Not changed here: it is 18's game, `spill` reads `power@self`
too, and the fix wants that track's own tests around it.

### Equality is two clamped subtractions, so a branch is a multiplication

Follow-suit needs "is this card's suit the led one" as a number. `|a - b|` has no
spelling and does not need one: subtract each way with a floor of zero, take
both away from 1, and what is left is 1 exactly when they were equal. That flag
then *multiplies* the value, which is how the whole of "what would this card win
with" is written without a branch:

```
live    = 1 - max(0, suit - led) - max(0, led - suit)   followed the suit
live    = min(1, live + trump)                          ...or is a rocket
contend = (value + 100 x trump) x live
```

Sixteen actions on a tag the trick zone hands out, and the trick winner is then
the one card whose `contend` fell short of the best by nothing — `gap` at zero,
read as an ordinary computed tag. **`max:` was never the missing piece**, exactly
as the analysis above said; the missing piece was naming the seat, and the
narrowing the analysis expected to need one authored clause per led suit turned
out to need none at all, because the led suit is a *number* the cards compare
themselves against rather than a scope name to be chosen between.

### A tag cannot see a hand, so the commander is asked seat by seat

`tags.find_targets` searches grid zones only (`{ grid = true }`), so
`@rocket_4` — or any tag scope — reaches nothing in a hand. There is no way to
ask "whose hand holds this card" in one condition, and the commander is exactly
that question.

What works is to ask it once per seat, of the seat itself:

```json
"set_active_seat:north_side", "stat_set:has_r4@mine.player:card:rocket_4@mine.hand",
"set_active_seat:east_side",  "stat_set:has_r4@mine.player:card:rocket_4@mine.hand",
"set_active_seat:south_side", "stat_set:has_r4@mine.player:card:rocket_4@mine.hand",
"set_active_seat:commander"
```

`card:<key>@mine.hand` works because a *zone* scope is not restricted to grids —
only a *tag* scope is — so the answer is written as an ordinary stat on the seat
card, and `commander` is a computed tag over it. Every later rule then names the
commander in one word, and the walk happens once.

This is [06](06-schema-and-types.md)'s "a face-up deck is still unsearchable"
arriving from a new direction: the exclusion is not about decks, it is that
**`count:<tag>` only sees a board**. Two idioms fall out and both are worth
keeping — *narrow with the zone and count the tag*, and *walk the seats to write
a stat, then make the answer a computed tag*.

> **06 shipped `@everywhere` for this (2026-08-23), and the seat-walk here still
> stands.** The new word counts a tag across hidden zones — but it answers *how
> many, anywhere*, not *whose*. The commander is a question about *which* seat
> holds the card, which is per-seat by nature, so `card:rocket_4@mine.hand`
> walked over the seats remains the right shape. `@everywhere` retires the *third*
> idiom nobody wrote — enumerating every zone by hand — not this one.

The walk is also the only way to deal: **there is no word for "every seat in
turn" outside a phase**, and `seat: "next"` is ignored on an `automatic` one
([23](23-splendor.md) found that), so a three-way deal is three pairs of actions
written out. Fine at four seats and clumsy at five.

### A card is born owned by where it was *created*, which a shared deck undoes

`cards.create` stamps `owner` from the zone a card is made in. The Crew deals
from one shared deck, so every playing card is unowned, and while it sits in a
hand `owner_of` answers by falling back to the hand's seat. That fallback
evaporates the instant the card is played into the shared trick — and "whose is
the winning card" is the whole game. One word fixes it, on every card's `play`:

```json
"action": ["set_owner:self:mine", "move_to:trick"]
```

The alternative the research proposed — a `per_seat` trick zone, so the seat
comes from the zone again — does not survive contact with `activate_zone`, which
resolves its argument to exactly **one** zone. A trick that has to be weighed as
a whole has to be one zone, so it is shared, and ownership has to be said.

### `activate_zone` runs a card's whole ability list, so two passes are two calls

The winner needs each card's `contend` (its own business) and then `best` (the
trick's), and a card cannot compute the second from the first in one sweep.
There is no way to run *one* of a card's abilities, so the answer is to run the
same ability twice with the phase-level line between:

```json
"activate_zone:trick",
"stat_set:best@each.trick:max:contend@trick",
"activate_zone:trick"
```

The ability is idempotent, so the first pass's `gap` is garbage nobody reads.
Cheap and honest, and it kept the whole calculation on one tag.

### A grid zone never drew its label

Found by looking rather than by testing, with the scratch screenshot harness
[07](07-presentation.md) records. `render.lua` drew a zone's `label` for stacks,
fans and decks and **not for grids**, so The Crew's three task rows, its offer
and its trick were all unnamed boxes. It was not this game's bug: LoR's `bench`,
Splendor's `nobles` and its `supply` ("The bank") have all named themselves since
they shipped and drawn nothing. Fixed, laid down before the cards so an empty row
says what it is waiting for and a full one covers it — which is what the `fan`
branch already said in a comment and only that branch did.

### The radio, built — and the five things it needed

**It works, and none of the five was about trick-taking.** One token a mission,
spent to lay a colour card face up and call it your highest, your lowest or your
only one of that colour; the card stays playable, stays bound by follow-suit,
and stays where you put it after it stops being true.

- **`ends_when`, so that saying something is not spending your turn.**
  `ends_after` counts plays and cannot tell one from another. The trick phases
  now say `"ends_when": "count:play_card@trick >= n"` — the turn ends when a card
  reaches the middle, and everything else a crew member may do leaves it alone.
- **A phase's `zone` as a list.** The open hand is a second place to play from,
  and `in_play_zone` took one zone. Normalised at the door into `zone_list`, with
  the first still the singular one (where a phase deals, what an overlay offers).
- **`min:`**, beside `sum:` and `max:`. It only ever sees the cards that carry
  the stat, which is the whole trick: give a pink card a `v_pink` and give no
  other card one, and `min:v_pink@mine.hand` is *the lowest pink I hold* — a
  question no scope can ask, because a tag reads grid zones only.
- **`face_up` on a hand.** The tag always claimed to override whatever the type
  would do, and hiding a hand is the only thing the type does there.
- **An ability that reaches nothing is not offered.** The rule existed for
  `moves` only; the radio has twelve abilities and a hand answers two or three,
  so the other nine were nine dead lines in the chooser.

Two things fell out that are worth keeping:

**"Only" is the other two agreeing.** An ability takes no `needs` — only a
card's `play` moment does — so `count:pink@mine.hand == 1` had nowhere to go,
and it turned out not to be needed: `max:v_pink@mine.hand <= min:v_pink@mine.hand`
is *I hold exactly one pink*, and it is the better sentence. (That an ability
cannot carry a `needs` is still a hole; it just was not this one's.)

**The escape hatch was per-zone, and two hands made it wrong.** `can_play`'s
hatch opens when nothing else in the card's own zone is playable. With a closed
hand and an open one, a lone gated card lying in the open hand would always
open it — which is follow-suit quietly switching itself off. It asks about
every zone the phase allows now.

### What is still left

The **order tokens** (`1`–`5`, `Ω`, `›`/`››`), which want a small authored graph
and a fourth loss check; the **printed fifty missions**, which this file replaces
with an opening overlay asking how many tasks the crew wants (one to five) rather
than claiming to be the logbook; **three and five players**, which only the seat
list and the rect arithmetic in `zones()` would have to agree about; and the
**two-player JARVIS variant**, which is a different game.

One deviation is deliberate and worth stating: the rulebook allows the radio
*before* a trick and never during one, and here it is usable on your own turn
until you play into the middle. That keeps every decision the token has — which
card, which claim, and which trick to spend it on — at the cost of letting a
later seat speak having seen the cards already played.

### The table has four sides, and the engine owns two corners

The first layout stacked three seats down the left with everything else beside
them, and it read as a list rather than as a table. Four crew members round a
rectangle is both the commoner game and the clearer picture: two hands along the
top edge, two along the bottom in reverse, so **the seat that follows you is the
one to your left on screen**. Four also divides forty, so the odd fourteenth card
that three seats leave in somebody's hand is gone.

Two rectangles are not the game's to use, and both were learnt by drawing them:
**the HUD writes into the top right** (phase label, then one line per visible
stat, growing downwards as stats are added) and **the event log into the bottom
left**. Nothing in `zones()` reaches into either, which is why the top row starts
at `y 0.17` and the bottom row stops at `y 0.895` rather than filling the edges.
